lesson.menu_title: What You Knew When You Decided
lesson.menu_desc: Telling the story of a decision instead of the outcome, and putting the events in the right order -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- What You Knew When You Decided
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 11 -- What You Knew When You Decided
lesson.grammar_point: past perfect and past perfect continuous

listenings.text: I sit on three boards and I interview a lot of finance people, and there is one thing I listen for that almost nobody prepares. It is not what you decided. Outcomes are luck as often as they are judgement, and anyway I can read the outcome. What I want is what you knew at the moment you decided, and what you did not know. A candidate who says we chose option B and it worked has told me nothing at all. A candidate who says we had been running two systems for eighteen months, we had modelled three scenarios, and the one thing we did not have was any visibility on the renewal, has told me how they think. And the second half of that matters more than the first. Naming what you did not know is the single most senior thing anybody does in an interview, and it is very rare, because it feels like admitting you were not in control. You were not in control. Nobody is.

By the time the board met in November, three things had already happened. We had lost the account in February, we had rebuilt the forecast twice, and we had been running the old reporting system alongside the new one for about eighteen months, which nobody had ever formally decided to do. So the decision in front of us was not really whether to cut. It was whether to cut before or after the renewal date, and the honest answer is that we did not know which way the renewal would go. What tipped it was the trade-off on cash. Cutting early cost us goodwill with two clients and bought us four months of visibility. I would take that trade again. What I did not know then, and I want to be clear about it, was that the market would soften in the second quarter, which made the decision look better than it was.

extra_audio.text: Margaret asks Fernando to describe a decision rather than a result. Fernando sets out what had already happened before the meeting. Fernando names the trade-off that decided it. Margaret asks what he did not know at that moment. Fernando names the one thing he could not see and says the outcome flattered the decision.
